Food Trip: Indulge · The Philippines · 03/67
Food Trip: Indulge · The PhilippinesThe Idea · 04/67

the ideaEight Filipino Worlds

Less a travel show than a series of entrances. Todd English walks into eight places that each cook a different answer to the same question.

The Philippines can carry a full season because it offers three layers at once: extraordinary food, dramatic landscapes, and a culture built around hospitality and gathering. This is not a conventional travel show. It is Todd English entering eight different Filipino worlds.

Every episode is engineered twice. Once as a 30-minute television hour that moves from a market at sunrise to a spa at sunset, and once as a digital machine: at least ten intentional short pieces per episode, shot during principal photography, never leftovers.

The season has a larger question, and it is the emotional spine of the show. Todd arrives in Manila thinking he knows the broad strokes. Every island changes the answer. By the final dinner under a volcano he understands that Filipino cuisine is not one cuisine. It is more than seven thousand islands telling different versions of the same story.

“Occasionally the 78-year-old woman making the greatest adobo you’ve ever tasted should be the celebrity.”

Food Trip: Indulge · The PhilippinesThe Host · 05/67

the hostTodd English in the Philippines

A chef who has cooked on four continents, whose last television food trip was Emmy-nominated, and who already feeds Manila.

Todd English is a five-time James Beard Award winner, the chef-restaurateur behind Olives, bluezoo, The Beast and Tuscany, and the co-founder of The English Hospitality Group. On television he has been a fixture for twenty-five years, from Cooking In with Todd English to Iron Chef and the PBS travel series Food Trip with Todd English, which earned him a Daytime Emmy nomination for Outstanding Lifestyle Host in 2008. This series is that format’s natural sequel: one chef, one country, eight worlds.

He is not a stranger here. Pound by Todd English serves his burgers at SM Mall of Asia, SM Megamall and SM City North EDSA, and his food hall concept opened at SM Aura in Taguig. The audience that queues for Pound is the audience that will watch him learn adobo from a grandmother in Binondo.

The Todd English lens

  • Fire and conviction · rustic Mediterranean technique meets a cuisine built on coals, vinegar and coconut.
  • Get involved · Todd on the lechon spit, at the batchoy pot, on the fishing boat, not on the sidelines.
  • The twist · every episode ends with Todd and a local chef reinterpreting what they learned, plated new.
  • Humour · “Can Todd handle Bicol?” The chili gets hotter; the show gets funnier.
  • Respect · the grandmother is the celebrity; the chef is the student.

Quick facts

  • Awards · 5 James Beard Awards; Bon Appétit Restaurateur of the Year
  • TV · PBS Food Trip with Todd English, Daytime Emmy nominee 2008
  • In the Philippines · Pound by Todd English, SM malls
  • Reach · @cheftoddenglish

Food Trip: Indulge · The PhilippinesWhy Now · 06/67

why nowThe Filipino Food Moment

Filipino food has stopped being a secret. The guides, the lists and the tourism board all arrived at the same time, and none of them has a television series yet.

Michelin arrives, 2025The inaugural MICHELIN Guide Manila & Environs and Cebu was unveiled on 30 October 2025: one two-star restaurant, eight one-stars, 25 Bib Gourmands, 108 establishments in all.
Asia’s 50 BestToyo Eatery in Makati ranked No. 42 on Asia’s 50 Best Restaurants 2025 and was named the Philippines’ best restaurant for the sixth time.
UNESCO Creative CitiesBaguio (crafts, 2017), Cebu (design, 2019), Iloilo (gastronomy, 2023). Two of the three are episodes of this season.
Filipino Food MonthEvery April, by Presidential Proclamation 469 (2018): a national platform the series can premiere into.
Love the PhilippinesThe Department of Tourism’s campaign since 2023, with 2026 targeting 6.4–6.8 million arrivals after 5.6 million in 2025. Food is the lever they have not fully pulled.
The diaspora is watching10.7 million overseas Filipinos; the world’s first Michelin-starred Filipino restaurant is in Chicago. Home is trending.

What nobody has made yet

  • A chef-led series that treats Filipino food as eight cuisines rather than one list of dishes.
  • A luxury frame for a country usually sold as budget travel: resorts, yachts, private dining, spa.
  • A diaspora product built for the 10.7 million who watch from abroad, not only for visitors.

Ready-made premiere moments

  • April · Filipino Food Month, a national platform for a launch.
  • January · Sinulog, Dinagyang and Ati-Atihan give three episodes a festival spine.
  • October · the annual Michelin Guide ceremony in Manila; the Manila episode’s chefs are on that list.

the valuesKain Tayo: The Words That Run the Table

Eight Filipino words the series will teach without a glossary, because every episode acts them out.

kain tayo / kumain ka na ba?"let's eat" / "have you eaten yet?" — the default Filipino greetingA Filipino host offers food before a guest can even ask, and "have you eaten?" doubles as "how are you?". On screen this is the show's open door: every household, market stall, or boat crew…
bayanihancommunal unity and mutual aid, from the image of neighbors literally carrying a house to a new location togetherBayanihan shows up as a whole barangay pitching in for a fiesta feast, a fishing catch split among boats, or a family's cooking passed hand to hand at a long table. It is the throughline…
pakikisamasmooth interpersonal relations; going along with the group to preserve harmonyPakikisama is why a market vendor will underprice a haggle rather than cause a scene, and why Todd will be handed a spoon and expected to try everything offered, refusal being mildly rude.…
utang na looba debt of gratitude, an internal moral debt repaid through loyalty rather than cashA grandmother who fed a whole generation of fishermen, or a chef who apprenticed under a mentor for free, describes the relationship in terms of utang na loob, not wages. It is the…
po / opo and manorespect particles added to speech for elders, and the gesture of pressing an elder's hand to one's foreheadAny grandmother, market elder, or fisherman patriarch on camera will be addressed with po/opo, and children (and often Todd, if coached) will mano before eating. It is a two-second gesture…
fiestathe patron-saint feast day, a town's biggest annual event: mass, procession, and an open table for anyone who walks inEvery barangay and town has one, and during fiesta the custom is an open house — strangers are fed. Iloilo's Ep5 and Bicol's Peñafrancia timing (Naga, mid-September) both hang directly off…
pasalubong & the balikbayan boxpasalubong: a gift brought home from a trip; the balikbayan box: the oversized corrugated box overseas Filipinos ship or carry home stuffed with goodsEvery domestic traveler carries pasalubong back to family; every OFW or emigrant fills a balikbayan box for the same reason at a bigger scale. It is the physical, shippable form of the…
merienda / the five meals a daymerienda: the afternoon (and sometimes mid-morning) snack meal; the Filipino day commonly runs breakfast, merienda, lunch, merienda, dinnerMerienda is where the pastries, halo-halo, and street snacks live — a distinct, unhurried meal, not a between-meals nibble. It gives the format a built-in fifth beat per day beyond the…

How the show uses them

  • Kain tayo opens every Last Table.
  • Lola is the celebrity when there is no celebrity.
  • Pasalubong is what Todd carries from island to island: the through-line prop.
  • Fiesta gives Iloilo, Cebu and Boracay their spine.

how Filipinos eatThe Culture of the Table

Not what is eaten, but how. The habits that make a Filipino meal recognisable from across the room.

Kamayan / boodle fightEating with bare hands off a banana-leaf-lined table piled with rice, grilled meats, and seafood, no individual plates. Originated as a Philippine military mess-hall practice ("boodle fight") and was adopted…
The rice-and-ulam plateRice is the constant; ulam ("the thing you eat with rice") is whatever protein or vegetable dish accompanies it — adobo, sinigang, grilled fish, a vegetable stew. The plate ratio (a mound of rice, a smaller…
Sawsawan — the condiment cultureSawsawan is the DIY dipping-sauce ritual at the center of the table: suka (cane or coconut vinegar, often spiced with chili and garlic), toyo (soy sauce) with calamansi, and bagoong (fermented shrimp or fish…
Carinderia / turo-turoA carinderia is a small, often family-run eatery with pre-cooked dishes displayed in trays; turo-turo ("point-point") describes the ordering method — you point at what you want rather than reading a menu. It…

Lechon as centrepieceA whole roasted pig, spit-fired until the skin cracks, is the Philippines' default centerpiece dish for any celebration worth having — and Cebu's version, seasoned inside the cavity rather than glazed on the…
Tuba / lambanog & the karaoke nightTuba is fermented coconut palm sap, drunk young and slightly sweet or aged and stronger; lambanog is its distilled, much higher-proof cousin, sometimes called "Filipino moonshine." Either one shows up wherever…

Episode 1 of 8 · Luzon

Manila: Old Soul, New City

Two Manilas in one meal: the world's oldest Chinatown and the country's newest skyline.

Metro Manila
Region
Metro Manila
Metro Manila (National Capital Region)
Gateway
NAIA, Manila
The season’s arrival city
Best months
Nov – Apr
Dry season; Jan–Apr driest and coolest. Wet season Jun–Nov brings street flooding in Binondo.
Signature
Lumpia · Pancit · Siopao
Roast meats · Adobo · Kare-kare · Kinilaw

Manila is the thesis statement. A city of fourteen million that eats Chinese, Spanish, American and Malay in the same meal, sometimes on the same plate. The episode moves between two Manilas: the 1594 Chinatown where Filipino-Chinese cooking was born, and the glass towers where a new generation of chefs is rewriting it.

Why this place
  • The opening statement of the season
  • Binondo: the oldest Chinatown in the world, founded 1594
  • Contemporary Filipino dining at its most serious
  • The skyline that sells the Indulge promise

the episodeManila: Run of Show

The seven movements of the formula, cast for this episode.

00:0002:00

Cold Open2 min

The halo-halo in extreme close-up: shaved ice, ube, leche flan, a spoon breaking through. Todd’s face. Cut to black.

02:0005:00

Arrival / Fantasy3 min

Skyline from the air at golden hour; hotel arrival; a cocktail with the city below. “I think I know this food.”

The People6 min

Ongpin Street at 7 a.m. with a Binondo historian or chef: the estero, fried siopao, the roast-meat windows, and the Filipino-Chinese family that has cooked here for generations.

In the family’s kitchen: adobo their way, kare-kare’s peanut sauce, lumpia rolled by hand. Todd learns that vinegar, not soy, is the spine.

17:0021:00

Indulge4 min

A rooftop pool, a private tasting with one of Manila’s serious contemporary chefs, and the after-dark side of the city.

21:0027:00

Todd Cooks6 min

Chef and Todd plate old Manila new: adobo-glazed short rib, charred eggplant, crispy garlic, coconut-vinegar jus.

27:0030:00

The Last Table3 min

An extravagant rooftop or private-dining dinner overlooking Manila; the Binondo family, the chef and the historian at one table.

Food Trip: Indulge · The PhilippinesEpisode 1 · The Table · 20/67

the foodManila: The Table

What is eaten here, what Todd learns, and how he answers it.

01
Lumpia

Fresh or fried spring roll wrapped in a thin crepe, filled with vegetables and/or meat.

02
Pancit

Stir-fried noodles, typically with vegetables, meat and/or shrimp.

03
Siopao

Steamed bun filled with meat, closely related to the Chinese baozi.

04
Roast meats (lechon macau / Chinese roast duck & pork)

Chinese-style roasted duck, pork belly (lechon macau) and char siu, sold whole or by the kilo from Binondo…

05
Adobo

Meat (usually pork and/or chicken) braised in vinegar, soy sauce, garlic, bay leaf and peppercorn.

06
Kare-kare

Oxtail and vegetable stew in a thick peanut sauce, served with sautéed shrimp paste (bagoong) on the side.

07
Kinilaw

Raw fish or seafood "cooked" in vinegar and citrus — the Filipino answer to ceviche.

08
Halo-halo

Shaved ice dessert with mixed sweet beans, fruits, jellies, ube (purple yam) ice cream and leche flan…

Todd’s twistthe reinterpretation

Adobo-glazed short rib, charred eggplant, crispy garlic, coconut vinegar jus.

The last table

Extravagant rooftop or private-dining dinner overlooking Manila.

Episode 2 of 8 · Luzon

Pampanga: Where Filipino Cooks Go to Eat

Culinary credibility beyond the beach — the province where the country's cooks go to eat.

Pampanga
Region
Pampanga
Pampanga
Gateway
Clark (CRK) or by road
1.5–2 h drive via NLEX–SCTEX
Best months
Nov – May
Cooler Dec–Feb; the Giant Lantern Festival lights San Fernando the week before Christmas.
Signature
Sisig · Kare-kare · Tocino
Bringhe · Tibok-tibok · Panecillos de San Nicolas · Turrones de Casuy

An hour north of Manila is the province Filipino cooks talk about the way Italians talk about Emilia-Romagna. Kapampangan food is the country’s most technical: slow, precise, unafraid of fat, and preserved almost entirely by women who never wrote anything down. This is the heritage cooking episode, and the one that gives the season its culinary credibility.

Why this place
  • The culinary capital of the Philippines
  • Sisig was invented here, in Angeles City
  • Heritage cooks still working from oral recipes
  • The family table as spectacle

The road north out of Manila: rice fields, Mount Arayat, a heritage house with a kitchen older than the republic.

05:0011:00

The People6 min

A public market at dawn, then an old family kitchen and a cook still preserving traditional Kapampangan technique. Recipes passed orally; the women who kept the cuisine alive.

11:0017:00

The Food Lesson6 min

Sisig from the pig’s head up; bringhe steamed in banana leaf; tibok-tibok set with carabao milk. Todd learns why nothing is wasted, and how a dish changes when it moves into a restaurant.

17:0021:00

Indulge4 min

Betis, the woodcarvers’ town and its baroque church; a heritage-house lunch; the lantern makers of San Fernando.

21:0027:00

Todd Cooks6 min

Composed sisig: charred calamansi, smoked pork belly and crackling, served in crispy lettuce cups. The heritage cook judges it.

27:0030:00

The Last Table3 min

A huge family table under the trees: three generations, twenty dishes, one province. Todd discovers the culinary soul of the country.

Cebu: Fire, Pig & Sea

The pig, the reef, and a city that designs with its hands.

Cebu
Region
Cebu
Cebu
Gateway
Mactan–Cebu (CEB)
1 h 30 direct flight
Best months
Jan – May
Least rain; Sinulog fills the city in mid-January, a spectacle or a crowd to avoid.
Signature
Cebu lechon · Sutukil · Kinilaw

Cebu is the Philippines at full volume: the roast pig visitors cross oceans for, a working harbour older than the Spanish, and a design scene UNESCO put on the map. This is the episode that smells of smoke. Open with the lechon, then move to the water.

Why this place

  • Seafood cooked at the water’s edge, sutukil style

the foodCebu: The Table

What is eaten here, what Todd learns, and how he answers it.

01
Cebu lechon

Whole pig stuffed with lemongrass (tanglad), garlic, green onion, bay leaf, star anise and sometimes saba…

02
Sutukil (sugba-tuwa-kilaw)

One catch cooked three ways at once: grilled (sugba), stewed (tuwa), and 'cooked' raw in vinegar (kilaw).

03
Kinilaw

Raw fish or seafood cut small and 'cooked' in local vinegar with onion, ginger and chili — the Visayan word…

04
Danggit / tuyo / dilis (dried fish)

Sun-dried, salted small fish — danggit is a butterfly-cut rabbitfish fried crisp; tuyo and dilis are smaller…

05
Swaki / tuyom (sea urchin)

Fresh sea urchin roe, eaten raw with vinegar, straight from the shell with a spoon.

Todd’s twistthe reinterpretation

Cebu lechon porchetta with lemongrass, garlic, calamansi and Filipino herb salsa; or crispy lechon bao with liver-sauce barbecue glaze.

The last table

Beach fire dinner.

Did you know

  • Cebu City was named a UNESCO Creative City of Design on October 30, 2019 — the second Philippine city in the network after Baguio.
  • Carbon Market has been trading since the early 1900s and hosts roughly 6,000 vendors, making it Cebu's oldest and largest public market.
  • Sinulog, Cebu's biggest festival honoring the Santo Niño, falls on the third Sunday of January (Jan 18, 2026) and draws 1.5-3 million people.

Breathing room: where Filipino ingredients actually come from.

Bohol
Region
Bohol
Bohol

Bohol gives the series breathing room. It is where ingredients come from: cacao drying in the sun, coconut split at the farm, fish wrapped in banana leaf. The Chocolate Hills are the postcard; the farms are the story. Nature, agriculture and quiet luxury.

Why this place

  • A UNESCO Global Geopark island

Iloilo: The Food City

A city too small to be famous, until UNESCO named it the food capital of the Philippines.

Iloilo City
Region
Iloilo City
Iloilo (Panay Island)
Gateway
Iloilo International (ILO)
1 h 15–1 h 30 direct flight
Best months
Nov – May
Dinagyang, the fourth Sunday of January, floods the city with fiesta food for two weeks before.
Signature
La Paz Batchoy · Pancit Molo · Chicken Inasal
Talaba · Managat · Tsokolate · Biscocho

In 2023 UNESCO named Iloilo a Creative City of Gastronomy, the first in the Philippines. Why a mid-sized river city? Because here food is a civic religion: a noodle soup invented in a market, dumplings named after a district, and a fiesta calendar that never ends. This episode should feel abundant.

Why this place
  • UNESCO Creative City of Gastronomy, 2023
  • La Paz batchoy and pancit molo were born here
  • Fiesta culture: long tables, family, music
  • Regional agriculture and the sweetest mangoes next door

Food Trip: Indulge · The PhilippinesEpisode 5 · The Table · 40/67

the foodIloilo: The Table

What is eaten here, what Todd learns, and how he answers it.

01
La Paz Batchoy

Miki noodle soup in pork-and-beef-bone broth topped with crushed chicharon, offal, and raw egg.

02
Pancit Molo

Wonton-style pork dumplings served in a clear chicken-and-pork broth, sometimes with shredded chicken.

03
Chicken Inasal (Ilonggo style)

Native chicken marinated in calamansi, vinegar, ginger and lemongrass, basted with annatto oil and chargrilled.

04
Talaba (grilled/baked oysters)

Fresh oysters from Iloilo Strait, grilled or baked with butter and cheese, or eaten raw with vinegar.

05
Managat (mangrove red snapper)

Whole reef fish, usually grilled or served sweet-and-sour.

06
Tsokolate (batirol hot chocolate)

Thick drinking chocolate whipped to a froth with a wooden batirol whisk, made from tableya (pure cacao tablets).

07
Biscocho / heritage baked goods

Twice-baked, butter-and-sugar toasted bread slices, plus piaya, barquillos and galletas.

08
Guimaras Mango

Sweet, golden carabao mango grown on the island 15-20 minutes offshore.

Todd’s twistthe reinterpretation

A luxurious batchoy: smoked pork broth, handmade noodles, crispy pork, bone marrow and calamansi. Not fancy for its own sake — how Todd interprets the flavors of the original market bowl.

The last table

A long fiesta table loaded with everything the episode touched — batchoy, pancit molo, chicken inasal, grilled talaba, Guimaras mangoes — family, music, and food everywhere, framed as the answer to 'why does a small city get a UNESCO food title?'

Did you know

  • Iloilo City became the first Philippine city named a UNESCO Creative City of Gastronomy, designated October 31, 2023.
  • Iloilo City has over 300 restaurants employing about 4,600 people in its gastronomy sector.
  • La Paz batchoy is credited to butcher Federico Guillergan Sr. at La Paz Public Market circa 1938.

Boracay: The Indulgence Episode

Where the Indulge title comes alive — earned with a fishing story, spent on a barefoot table on the sand.

Boracay Island
Region
Boracay Island
Aklan (Municipality of Malay)
Gateway
Caticlan (MPH) + banca
1 h flight, 10-min boat crossing
Best months
Nov – May
Amihan: flat calm seas on the west-facing White Beach and up to eight hours of sun a day Feb–May.
Signature
Grilled prawns · Chili crab · Whole grilled fish
Kinilaw · Tropical fruit · Beach barbecue · Inubarang manok

Four kilometres of white sand that the country closed for six months to save. This is where the Indulge title comes alive: paraw sails at sunset, spa, champagne, seafood. Then we earn it, with a fishing boat before light and a market where you buy the catch and carry it to a cook.

Why this place
  • The title episode
  • The most sponsor-friendly hour of the season
  • Buy-the-catch market culture
  • Amihan-season sunsets on White Beach

07
Episode 7 of 8 · Luzon

Palawan: Into Paradise

What does food taste like when civilisation almost disappears?

El Nido / Bacuit Bay
Region
El Nido / Bacuit Bay
Palawan
Gateway
El Nido (ENI) via Clark, or PPS
Clark–El Nido by air; PPS + 5 h road
Best months
Dec – May
Calmest seas for lagoon access; Aug–Oct typhoon risk can shut boat operations entirely.
Signature
Kinilaw · Tamilok · Lato
Grilled whole fish · Grilled prawns · Coconut seafood curry · Green mango with calamansi

Palawan is the counterpoint to Manila. The luxury is not chandeliers; the luxury is access to an almost impossible natural setting. Limestone cliffs rising out of jade water, a fisherman who knows which reef, and a fire on a beach with nobody else on it. What does food taste like when civilisation almost disappears?

Why this place
  • The cinematic masterpiece of the season
  • Repeatedly voted the most beautiful island in the world
  • Fire cooking with very little equipment
  • The deserted-beach dinner is the trailer

The Machine

One production. A television series, eighty short pieces, and an audience that spans the world.

Food Trip: Indulge · The Philippines · 58/67
Food Trip: Indulge · The PhilippinesThe Arc · 59/67

the arcWhat Is Filipino Food?

Not eight disconnected tourism commercials. One question, asked eight times, with the answer changing on every island.

ChineseNoodles, dumplings, soy, the roast-meat window. Binondo, 1594.
SpanishAdobo’s name, the fiesta table, leche flan, the sausages, the church calendar.
IndigenousKinilaw, fire, banana leaf, root crops, coconut in every form.
Pacific seafoodReef fish, sea urchin, crab, squid, the boat at dawn.
AmericanSweetness, canned milk, the burger, the hot dog, halo-halo’s ice.
CoconutGata, vinegar, oil, sugar, the tree that feeds every province.
VinegarThe spine of the cuisine: sour before salt, preservation before refrigeration.
FireLechon, inasal, the beach barbecue, the coal-lit street.
RiceThe plate every dish is built around, from garlic rice to charred boodle rice.
PreservationBagoong, tuyo, tocino, tapa: salt, sun and sugar as survival.
FamilyRecipes carried in hands, not books. The grandmother is the celebrity.
7,641 islandsOne question, thousands of answers. Each episode changes it.
  1. 01ManilaTodd thinks he knows adobo. He learns vinegar is the spine and Chinatown is the root.
  2. 02PampangaTechnique. The most exacting cooks in the country, and none of them wrote it down.
  3. 03CebuFire and salt water. The pig and the reef, and design as a way of life.
  4. 04BoholOrigins. Cacao, coconut and the farm before the restaurant.
  5. 05IloiloCivic pride. A city that made food its identity and earned UNESCO’s name for it.
  6. 06BoracayIndulgence, earned. The catch first, then the champagne.
  7. 07PalawanAccess as luxury. Fire on a beach, no equipment, nothing else needed.
  8. 08BicolHeat. The final answer: Filipino food is not one cuisine, it is a conversation between islands.
By Episode 8 Todd realises Filipino cuisine isn’t one cuisine. It’s 7,641 islands telling different versions of the same story. That gives the show emotional intelligence.

Rules of the engine

  • Shot on purpose · every piece is on the call sheet; none are leftovers.
  • Vertical first · a second camera frames 9:16 in every food-lesson and first-bite moment.
  • Every maker gets a piece · the grandmother, the fisherman and the carver each leave with their own film.
  • Sequenced to the island · the week an episode airs, its ten pieces are the only pieces posted.

For the millions who live abroad the series is not a destination pitch. It is the food of home, cooked by the people who never left, with a guest learning it for the first time.

Why it matters to the show

  • Facebook remains a primary channel for Filipino audiences abroad.
  • Remittances of $39.6B a year say how tightly the diaspora stays connected.
  • Filipino food is rising in the US: Michelin stars, mainstream adobo, a generation of Filipino-American chefs.
  • Social media: Filipinos are among the world’s heaviest users at 4h 50m a day.
  • Balikbayan · the homecoming is a cultural institution; the series is a homecoming you can stream.

The Filipino food moment abroad

  • Kasama, Chicago · the world’s first Michelin-starred Filipino restaurant (2022), since promoted to two stars.
  • California · 1.7 million Filipino Americans, about 38% of the US total; Hawaii has the highest share of any state.
  • iWant (formerly iWantTFC) · ABS-CBN’s diaspora streaming service, still operating in 2026: a ready window.

“Not only come visit the Philippines. It’s come home through food.”

Food Trip: Indulge · The PhilippinesProduction · 64/67

the planWhen and How to Shoot

The dry season, November to May, is the window for all eight hubs. Fiesta dates fix Iloilo and Cebu in January; the Giant Lantern Festival fixes Pampanga in December.

JanSinulog · Dinagyang · Ati-Atihan
FebPeak dry
MarPeak dry
AprFilipino Food Month
MayHot · mango season
JunHabagat begins
JulWet
AugIbalong · wet
SepPeñafrancia · typhoon peak
OctMichelin · typhoon risk
NovAmihan returns
DecGiant Lantern Festival
Dry season · shoot windowWet season · typhoon exposure

Logistics

  • Gateway · Manila (NAIA); Clark for Pampanga. Domestic legs by Philippine Airlines and Cebu Pacific; El Nido flights now fly under Cebgo and Manila–El Nido moved to Clark in March 2026.
  • Furthest hop · every hub is under 90 minutes by air from Manila or Clark.
  • Language · English is an official language; crews, chefs and fixers work in English.

Incentives & partners

  • FDCP FilmPhilippines · Film Location Incentive Program: a 20% cash rebate up to ₱25M (about $450K) for international projects using a Filipino line-production company, plus a possible 5% cultural bonus. Confirm 2026 cycle dates.
  • Department of Tourism · Love the Philippines; food-tourism push.
  • Windows · Philippine broadcasters and streamers; iWant for the diaspora.

Proposed shoot · two blocks (for discussion)

  • Block A · January · Cebu (Sinulog) → Bohol → Iloilo (Dinagyang) → Boracay (Ati-Atihan next door): four Visayan episodes inside one festival month, four shoot days each plus travel.
  • Block B · February–March · Manila → Pampanga → Palawan → Bicol: calm seas for El Nido, clearest skies for Mayon, Manila last for the contemporary-chef dinners.
  • Total · about 40 shoot days, 8 travel days, one crew, one second unit for the vertical engine.

Sensitivities & permits

  • Boracay · post-rehabilitation rules govern beach dining; the sunset table needs a permit and a compliant resort frontage.
  • El Nido · protected-area zoning; island cooking by arrangement with the LGU and resort partners.
  • Mayon · PHIVOLCS alert level and the 6-km danger zone decide how close the finale sits.
  • Indigenous communities · consent first, credit on screen.

the wordsA Short Filipino Food Vocabulary

The words that recur across all eight episodes.

Adobo
Meat braised in vinegar, garlic, soy and bay: the national dish with a Spanish name and a native method.
Bagoong
Fermented shrimp or fish paste; the salt of kare-kare.
Batchoy
Iloilo noodle soup with pork, offal and chicharrón.
Bicol Express
Pork and chili stewed in coconut milk.
Boodle / kamayan
A feast laid on banana leaves, eaten by hand.
Calamansi
The small, sharp Philippine lime.
Carinderia
A neighbourhood eatery with pots on display.
Fiesta
A town or barangay feast day; the whole street cooks.
Gata
Coconut milk.
Halo-halo
“Mix-mix”: shaved ice, sweet beans, fruit, ube, leche flan.
Inasal
Chicken grilled over coals with annatto and calamansi.
Kare-kare
Oxtail in peanut sauce, served with bagoong.
Kinilaw
Raw fish cured in vinegar, ginger and chili.
Laing
Dried taro leaves cooked down in coconut milk and chili.
Lambanog / tuba
Coconut spirit; palm wine.
Lechon
Whole spit-roasted pig; Cebu’s is stuffed with lemongrass.
Lola
Grandmother; the keeper of the recipe.
Lumpia
Spring roll, fresh or fried.
Merienda
The afternoon snack meal.
Pancit
Noodles, in dozens of regional forms.
Pancit molo
Pork dumpling soup from Molo, Iloilo.
Pandesal
The morning bread roll.
Pasalubong
The gift you bring home from a trip.
Patis / suka
Fish sauce / vinegar: the two table condiments.
Pili
The Bicol nut, richer than a macadamia.
Pinangat
Taro leaves wrapped around fish or pork, simmered in coconut milk.
Sawsawan
The dipping sauce you mix yourself.
Sili
Chili; siling labuyo is the small hot one.
Silog
Garlic rice and egg with a cured meat: tapsilog, tocilog.
Sinigang
Sour tamarind soup.
Siopao
Steamed filled bun, from the Chinese baozi.
Sisig
Chopped pig’s head and liver on a sizzling plate; invented in Pampanga.
Tablea
Roasted cacao tablets for hot chocolate.
Tocino
Sweet-cured pork, a Pampanga specialty.
Turo-turo
“Point-point”: choose your food from the pots.
Ube
Purple yam.
